about: How each place's parties choose their candidates for the general election, as the law stood in 2026: the method (a party primary, an all-party top-two or top-four primary), the standing date rule and the 2026 date actually set, and any runoff. Read by simulation/nominations/nomination-rules.ts. A field without a directly read value is initialized from the closest real rule and marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE with its basis and comparison places; absence never means zero or "no." South Carolina and Virginia let each party choose its method (partyMayChooseMethod); every party starts with a primary until the game has party officers to make that choice. A law enacted in play changes the date rule or the method through the rule-change reader (office key us-xx-election-law).

partyMayChooseMethod.ruleText: The state party chooses the method for U.S. Senate and statewide offices; the district, county or city party chooses for other offices. A General Assembly seat with one incumbent of the party uses the method that incumbent designates. For any other office, a party whose last nominee won a primary (or was unopposed in one) and then the general election must nominate by primary unless all its incumbents for that office consent to another method. Otherwise the party decides.
